This vignette introduces deterministic cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) using
the Sick-Sicker Markov model as a running example. It covers the core concepts
of incremental analysis, dominance, the cost-effectiveness frontier, tornado
diagrams, threshold analysis, and discounting.

## Background

Cost-effectiveness analysis compares interventions by their incremental cost
per unit of health outcome gained, typically expressed as the **Incremental
Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER)**:

$$\text{ICER} = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta E} = \frac{C_1 - C_0}{E_1 - E_0}$$

where $C$ and $E$ denote costs and effects (QALYs), and subscripts 0 and 1
denote the comparator and the intervention (Drummond et al., 2015). A strategy
is considered cost-effective if its ICER falls below the decision-maker's
**willingness-to-pay (WTP)** threshold.

An equivalent formulation uses the **Incremental Net Monetary Benefit (INB)**:

$$\text{INB} = \lambda \cdot \Delta E - \Delta C$$

where $\lambda$ is the WTP threshold. A positive INB indicates
cost-effectiveness at that threshold (Stinnett & Mullahy, 1998).

## Setup

```{r load}
library(ShinyCEA)
m <- cea_sick_sicker()
print(m)
```

The Sick-Sicker model is a 4-state Markov cohort model (Healthy, Sick, Sicker,
Dead) with 5 strategies: standard of care and 4 treatments that modify
progression and mortality via relative risks. This model structure follows the
DARTH Group's pedagogical framework (Alarid-Escudero et al., 2019).

## Running the Deterministic Analysis

```{r deterministic}
det <- run_deterministic(m, m$default_params(), wtp = 100000)
det$table[, c("Strategy", "Cost", "QALY", "NMB", "ICER_vsRef")]
```

`run_deterministic()` simulates all strategies at their base-case parameter
values, computes NMB at the specified WTP, and auto-selects the reference
strategy (highest NMB):

```{r ref}
cat("Reference strategy:", det$ref)
```

You can override the reference with `ref_strategy = "std"` to compute
incremental values against a specific comparator.

## Dominance and the Cost-Effectiveness Frontier

When comparing multiple strategies, some may be **dominated** --- they cost
more and produce fewer QALYs than an alternative. Others may be **extendedly
dominated** --- they lie above the line connecting two other strategies on the
cost-effectiveness plane, meaning a mix of those strategies would be preferred
(Drummond et al., 2015).

`frontier_analysis()` classifies every strategy:

```{r frontier-table}
det$frontier_status[, c("Strategy", "Cost", "QALY", "Status")]
```

The frontier plot connects non-dominated strategies with a dashed line:

```{r frontier-plot}
plot_frontier(det$frontier_status, palette = cea_palette("uw"))
```

Sequential ICERs along the frontier represent the cost per additional QALY of
moving from one efficient strategy to the next more effective (and more costly)
one:

```{r icers}
det$icers
```

## Tornado Diagram (One-Way Sensitivity Analysis)

Deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) varies one parameter at a time
between its lower and upper bounds while holding all others at base case. The
tornado diagram ranks parameters by their impact on a chosen metric (Briggs
et al., 2012).

```{r tornado}
df_tor <- m$default_params()
df_tor <- df_tor[df_tor$include_tornado & (is.finite(df_tor$lower) | is.finite(df_tor$upper)), ]

tor <- build_tornado_data(df_tor, det$pars, m,
                          ref = "std", target = "t4",
                          metric = "INB", wtp = 100000)

plot_tornado(tor, base_val = unique(tor$base)[1],
             metric_label = "INB (t4 vs std)",
             title = "One-Way Sensitivity: t4 vs std")
```

Parameters at the top of the tornado have the largest influence on the
decision. The two colors represent the lower and upper bounds of each
parameter --- if both bars extend in the same direction, the parameter has a
monotone effect on the metric.

## Threshold Analysis

Threshold analysis identifies the parameter value at which the decision
changes --- where ICER equals WTP, or equivalently, where INB crosses zero
(Fenwick et al., 2006).

```{r threshold}
thr <- threshold_analysis(m, det$pars, param_name = "drug_t4",
                          ref = "std", target = "t4",
                          range_min = 0, range_max = 5000,
                          n_points = 50, wtp = 100000, mode = "inb")

cat("Threshold drug cost:", round(thr$threshold, 2))
```

```{r threshold-plot}
plot_threshold(thr$grid, thr$threshold, param_name = "drug_t4",
               wtp = 100000, mode = "inb")
```

The threshold value tells the decision-maker the maximum drug cost at which
the intervention remains cost-effective.

## Discounting

Discounting reflects time preference --- a QALY gained today is worth more
than one gained in the future. Most HTA guidelines recommend 3% annual
discounting for both costs and health outcomes (Weinstein et al., 1996;
NICE, 2022).

The bundled models include `d_cost` and `d_qaly` parameters (default 3%).
Compare discounted vs. undiscounted results:

```{r discounting}
params_no_disc <- m$default_params()
params_no_disc$base[params_no_disc$name == "d_cost"] <- 0
params_no_disc$base[params_no_disc$name == "d_qaly"] <- 0

det_no <- run_deterministic(m, params_no_disc, wtp = 100000)

comparison <- data.frame(
  Scenario = c("3% discounting", "No discounting"),
  Cost_std = c(det$table$Cost[det$table$Strategy == "std"],
               det_no$table$Cost[det_no$table$Strategy == "std"]),
  QALY_std = c(det$table$QALY[det$table$Strategy == "std"],
               det_no$table$QALY[det_no$table$Strategy == "std"])
)
comparison
```

`cea_discount_weights()` generates the per-cycle discount vector used
internally:

```{r discount-weights}
# 10 annual cycles at 3%
w <- cea_discount_weights(10, rate = 0.03, cycle_length = 1)
round(w, 4)
```

## Health Checks

Before running analyses, validate the model and parameters:

```{r health}
health <- validate_params_and_model(m, m$default_params())
health[, c("check", "status")]
```

This checks parameter table completeness, distribution validity, bounds
consistency, and whether each strategy simulates successfully with finite
cost and QALY.
